Messages.Author: baa01308
Messages.Body:
np...@umich.edu (Neil Paananen) wrote:
>I've heard a couple of Trap explanations, but I have a feeling that I'm not going
>to totally understand it until someone gives me a good example of it. If I am
>understanding it correctly it is a VERY powerful card... A press anytime any
>methuselah plays any card??? Well, an example would be greatly appreciated.
>

It can be a powerful card, but it pays to understand how it works before you try to
use it. Here's an example of a Trap sprung on me:

Black Cat, armed with a magnum, intercepts Sir Walter Nash's action. Nash is
unarmed. BC has 5 blood and Nash has 7 blood at the beginning of combat. Nash's
Methuselah declines to play pre-maneuver cards, but BC's Methuselah plays Trap.
Now neither Methuselah may play any new cards for the next three rounds of combat.
Note, however, that cards *already* played remain effective.

Round 1: BC uses the magnum to maneuver to long range. Nash strikes with fist;
BC uses the magnum. BC remains at 5 blood, and Nash is down to 5 blood. Trap
provides BC with a press to continue combat.

Round 2: Neither vampire maneuvers. Nash strikes with fist; BC uses the magnum.
BC is down to 4 blood and Nash is down to 3 blood. Trap provides BC with a press
to continue combat.

Round 3: Neither vampire maneuvers. Nash strikes with fist; BC uses the magnum.
BC is down to 3 blood and Nash is down to 1 blood. Trap provides BC with a press
to continue combat.

Cards may be played (including another Trap) as of the beginning of Round 4.

Round 4: Neither vampire maneuvers. Nash plays Majesty, ending combat.

I was lucky BC's Methuselah did not have a Manstopper Rounds at the beginning of
combat (he had some in his library). If he did, he could have played it on BC
before springing the Trap, and Nash would have gone to torpor.

As you can see, Trap is especially powerful in a weapons deck because it
deprives your opponent of all strike cards for three rounds of combat. You could,
for example, arm a 3-blood vampire with a bastard sword and easily send bigger
vampires with only 4 or 5 blood right to torpor, without seriously caring what
happens to your own. You do even better with a flak jacket. I suppose, with the
right cards, Trap would also work with a potence deck--say, if you play Torn
Signpost or its equivalent before the Trap.

It is important to remember that the acting vampire has first dibs on playing
pre-maneuver cards. As a result, Trap is even more effective when played by an
acting vampire, as it precludes any plays whatsoever by the reacting vampire. If
you are the reacting vampire and want to play Trap, be sure to allow your opponent
to decline to play pre-maneuver cards before springing the Trap. Of course,
playing Trap when the target has the means to hit back is not necessarily wise
(magnum slugfests are costly, and often help spectator Methuselahs more than the
participants). Also, it is of no particular benefit to use Trap on someone with a
Hawg, who can use it for a press to end combat notwithstanding the press to
continue provided free by the Trap.

Hope this helps. Good luck!

Bruce Goldstein

: Black Cat, armed with a magnum, intercepts Sir Walter Nash's action.
Nash is
: unarmed. BC has 5 blood and Nash has 7 blood at the beginning of
combat. Nash's
: Methuselah declines to play pre-maneuver cards, but BC's Methuselah
plays Trap.
: Now neither Methuselah may play any new cards for the next three rounds
of combat.
: Note, however, that cards *already* played remain effective.

Well, this is not how Trap works. Trap does not restrict the playing of
cards by Meths during the combat. Instead it gives a press to continue
combat until 3 consecutive rounds occur where neither Meth plays a card.
That means there will be 4 presses (because the round where the Trap was
played counts as a round where a card was played.)

So when 3 consecutive rounds occur without withr Meth playing cards, then
the Trap presses stop. Whenever a Meth plays a card, the counter for Tap
presses resets to 0.

So if BC and Nash hit each other for 4 rounds and do nothing else, then
the Trap stops providing presses.

But if BC and Nash hit each other for 3 rounds, and then BC plays an
additional strike card in the fourth round of combat, there will be
another 3 rounds of the Trap providing presses.

The upshot of the trap is that in most cases the combat goes on until
someone is in torpor, or until someone plays a press to counter the Trap's
press to continue. This is not always the case, but most times I have
seen it work that way.

Any card played by either vamp during the combat resets the press counter,
whether it is a manuever card, a damage prevention card, a strike card,
and additional strike card...whatever.

Sorry this is a little rambling. The point is that all the Trap does is
provide a series of presses to continue combat. It does not limit or
restrict the cards that either Meth/vamp can play. But if cards are
played, then it increases the number of presses to continue that the Trap
provides. These presses to continue can be countered by either Meth/vamp,
and if there are no more presses to continue, then the combat ends.

I hope this helps.

stephen beaulieu

It is an easy interpretation of the admittedly ambiguous text on trap:

Trap Combat
Combat automatically has a press, only usable to continue combat each
round. This continues until 3 rounds of combat pass with no cards being
played by any Methuselah. Only usable before range is determined on the
first round.
Artist: Jeff Rebner

3 rounds *with no cards being played*.

WotC made a ruling that explained the card a little better, but that doesn't
remedy the ambiguity present in the card text.
